articles.title: Chinese App Ecosystem Blocks On-Device AI Assistants from Operating Systems
articles.content: Over 150 Chinese Apps Deny AI Assistant’s Use on Smartphone The response to the release of a cutting-edge AI-powered smartphone has highlighted the industry’s dependence on other companies being willing to cooperate with new tech. By Chen Yiru Oct 19, 2026 # artificial intelligence # technology More than 150 Chinese apps have forbidden ByteDance’s mobile AI assistant Doubao from operating them on smartphone manufacturer Nubia Technology’s newly released agentic AI smartphone. In a list published Oct. 14 on Doubao’s official account on messaging app WeChat, its developers identified dozens of apps that prohibit its graphical user interface (GUI) automation. The technology interprets a user’s spoken command, reads what is displayed on their smartphone’s screen, and navigates across and operates apps to complete the task.  Doubao had released its Smart Assistant Execution Protocol on Sept. 14, giving developers one month to decide whether to let the assistant operate their apps. Apps owned by ByteDance’s rival technology companies Tencent and Alibaba make up nearly 60% of the list, including WeChat from the former and digital payment system Alipay from the latter, according to domestic media outlet Cailian Press. Others include those from e-commerce giant Meituan, ride-hailing platform Didi, lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, e-commerce platform Pinduoduo, China’s three state-run telecommunications carriers, several banks, and rival AI apps DeepSeek and Kimi. The listed apps can still be installed and used manually. Absent from the list are e-commerce giant JD.com and most apps from internet service company Baidu, with the exception of Baidu Maps. A Baidu employee told domestic media outlet Caijing magazine that the phone’s shipment volume remains too small to pose a meaningful concern for the company. Nubia bills the NaviX Ultra as “the world’s first AI-powered smartphone,” bringing agentic AI to consumers. The company, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, said that within seconds of the smartphone’s Sept. 16 launch, it generated 100 million yuan ($15 million) in sales. The phone’s price starts at 5,999 yuan. Nubia released a prototype of the current AI phone, the M153, for 3,499 yuan in December last year. Though it quickly sold out, users soon reported that whenever the assistant attempted to operate WeChat, they were automatically logged out of the app. Doubao’s developers later disabled the assistant’s ability to operate the super app. On the same day Doubao published the list of restricted apps, Nubia announced a software update — including improved localized data search, call-recording summaries, and call screening functions — and offered users six months of free Doubao membership, worth roughly 400 yuan. As of Monday, none of the included app developers have commented publicly on the news. Liu Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University’s Institute for National Strategic Studies, told Cailian Press that China has no regulations relating to how AI agents operate third-party applications.  Given the lack of oversight, Liu said, it is understandable that developers would deny such access over data security and user privacy concerns. He added that their resistance may also reflect a desire to protect their own AI ecosystems, particularly given Doubao’s already vast user base. In its post, Doubao’s developers stated that other apps can opt out of its GUI technology at any time, and its list of cooperating companies would be updated every Wednesday. Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson. (Header image: VCG)

articles.title: Trump Appointees Pressured Federal Cybersecurity Officials to Breach Voting Systems
articles.content: An Unusual Request: Political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security wanted the agency that protects election systems to get and hack a voting machine, which shocked staffers. Undermining Election Security: President Donald Trump has said voting is vulnerable even as his administration has undermined the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is supposed to protect it. On Their Own: Election officials across the country say the Trump administration’s attacks on CISA have left them to solve security issues with the midterms approaching. These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story. A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it. The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request.  The proposition was shocking to CISA’s career staffers, according to one of the former officials. CISA typically worked to thwart hackers. Moreover, the agency had been directed not to alert the voting machine company if it uncovered flaws, contrary to its standard practices. The request made the CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. “My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any [election] results they don’t like,” one of the former officials said. “This goes against everything CISA represents.” The CISA employees repeatedly told the political appointees that their request was impossible, in part because the agents capable of pulling off such an operation had just been laid off by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative. The appointees eventually stopped pressing CISA. Though not acted on, the request shows how the Trump administration has tried to use the agency for its own ends while draining it of resources for one of its critical missions: protecting the nation’s voting systems.  In Trump’s second term, his administration has laid off or pushed out more than 1,000 CISA employees, shrinking the agency by about one-third. The president’s 2027 budget proposal would reduce funding for the agency by another $700 million, which could necessitate 900 additional layoffs.  In response, Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation into CISA’s ability to do its job and demanded answers as to why federal funds are not being used to support election security as directed by Congress. Since Trump signed the CISA Act in 2018, the agency has worked with state authorities and voting machine vendors to help protect election infrastructure from cyberattacks. During Trump’s second term, though, CISA has abandoned much of this work. Several state election authorities said the agency provided them no assistance — and no explanation for its absence — during the most critical planning stages for the upcoming midterms. “There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as a consultant for CISA. In 2025 and through mid-September 2026 — when the bulk of preparations for the election typically would have been completed — “they were nonexistent. Literally nonexistent.” While Trump has repeatedly warned that America’s elections are vulnerable to hacking, in some cases repeating disproven claims, experts said his administration is undermining the federal government’s role in helping secure them. Though CISA re-emerged in September with a last-minute security plan for the election, some state officials told ProPublica they fear that what is left of the agency has been compromised by a conspiracy-obsessed presidential administration. In recent months, in reviving debunked theories about the 2020 election, the Trump administration has declassified troves of records, including sensitive material that state officials provided to CISA. Some state authorities said they no longer trusted the administration enough to share information with CISA, a key to the agency’s success in past elections. “They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing relationship,” said one former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who now advises state governments on national security. “There’s no fucking way they’re ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.”  A spokesperson for the White House declined an interview request but defended Trump’s handling of election security in an emailed statement. “President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections,” said Lauren Bis.  Bis referred specific questions about CISA’s handling of elections to DHS. DHS and CISA did not respond to interview requests or to a detailed list of questions. “There’s no fucking way [state governments are] ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.” A former federal cybersecurity official who advises state governments Current and former CISA employees and state election officials describe an agency that has become significantly less equipped to help states fight legitimate cyber threats. State leaders say they have used their own resources to shore up gaps left by CISA, such as paying for sensor technology that can detect unusual activity in election networks. But some services, like intel on foreign actors, can’t be replicated. Some people interviewed said they were worried that Trump and his allies continue to ratchet up rhetoric about voting security, particularly about threats to voting machines. Officials in one large voting jurisdiction said they have met privately with machine vendors to come up with a contingency plan if the federal government seizes their machines or declares them unusable. “I don’t pay attention to what the president says. I pay attention to what his administration does,” Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said. “And what they’ve done is basically cut us off and left us on our own.” Defending elections from hackers wasn’t always part of DHS’s remit. Throughout the mid-1990s and 2000s, a series of cyberattacks rocked the federal government, demonstrating the emerging threat. In 2007, hackers broke into the Pentagon and stole terabytes of sensitive data. The digital heist, by an unknown foreign adversary, was so damaging that one intelligence leader later described it as an “espionage Pearl Harbor.” Under George W. Bush, DHS underwent a reorganization to more effectively combat terrorism and respond to disasters like Hurricane Katrina. The department dedicated resources under an office called the National Protection and Programs Directorate to help fortify advanced cyber defense systems and important infrastructure. The office’s work ranged from helping secure events like the Super Bowl to protecting chemical plants to issuing cybersecurity warnings to the private sector and the public. In 2018, Trump signed a bill making the office a stand-alone agency, allowing for more federal funding and transforming it into, essentially, the ultimate tech support desk for anything DHS designated “critical infrastructure.” The bill renamed the agency CISA. Though Trump helped create CISA, he didn’t much appreciate the work the agency did under its old name to expose the extent of Russia’s meddling in the 2016 presidential election. Russian agents had unleashed a massive disinformation campaign, with a Kremlin-backed troll farm creating thousands of social media accounts posing as Americans and promoting Trump, according to bipartisan reports from the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence released before the 2020 election. A dozen Russian military agents were indicted for what the Justice Department described as “a sustained effort to hack into the computer networks of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the Democratic National Committee, and the presidential campaign of Hillary Clinton.” Trump publicly downplayed this interference, but DHS leadership saw the Russia attack as an escalation. In January 2017, before Trump took office, DHS upgraded America’s elections to the status of critical infrastructure. This placed the polls and all voting technology used in federal elections under the watch of what would soon become CISA.  To carry out this function, CISA needed help. But states and voting machine vendors were wary about sharing data on weaknesses in voting systems, fearing it could be exploited if certain details were to become public. State officials were also reluctant to cede any role in election preparation to the federal government. Gradually, though, CISA and state election officials negotiated a fragile trust. At its center was a commitment: The sensitive information states and vendors shared with CISA would be kept confidential. “It took years and years of building trust, of talking to election officials, of hiring people with elections experience who could be validators for the work that CISA wanted to do, before they finally built strong working relationships,” said Derek Tisler, who specializes in election security as counsel for the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan institute based out of New York University School of Law. Under Director Chris Krebs, CISA hosted penetration testing in which its agents would try to hack into a state’s system to locate weaknesses that could then be patched, along with tabletop exercises simulating a series of potential catastrophes around elections. CISA also offered regular secret-level briefings to secretaries of state to share federal intelligence. And CISA paid for sensor technology that looked for potential malicious online activity on election networks, notifying officials about emerging threats. “The staffing was there, the expertise was there, the visibility was there, the funding was there,” Macias said. The consortium shared data as run of the mill as spambots as well as more serious threats. If Virginia caught unusual activity in its system, it could let other states know to be vigilant.  While CISA had prepared for attacks from the Chinese and Russian governments, or lone wolf hackers, few there had expected the threat to elections would come from inside the White House. But when Trump refused to concede to Joe Biden in 2020, claiming the vote had been rigged, CISA became a key component of the guardrails that ultimately led to the election results being certified. The agency, in a statement co-signed by secretaries of state and voting machine vendors, vouched for the election’s integrity, calling it “the most secure in American history.” When Krebs publicly rebutted claims amplified by the White House as “unsubstantiated” or “technically incoherent,” Trump fired him over Twitter. As Congress prepared to vote on certifying the election results, it was members of CISA, along with the FBI, who convinced then-Attorney General Bill Barr that the conspiracy theories embraced by the president could be explained by human error, not systemic fraud or hacking. When Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, his administration immediately started to dismantle CISA. The administrative notices were sent out just a couple of weeks after the inauguration and included the team in charge of dispelling disinformation. For the employees under the DOGE microscope, work became impossible, said one former senior CISA employee. “Those groups couldn’t even order a pizza.”  DOGE laid off people critical to the agency’s election work, including those who’d worked closely with states. The Trump administration cut funding for the technology that monitored web and election servers, blinding the federal government to breaches it had detected. When it came time for states to prepare for the 2026 midterms, CISA had disappeared. On the evening of July 16, in the Black Hills of South Dakota, dozens of election officials and their staffs gathered for a reception near Mount Rushmore. It was the third night of an annual conference for secretaries of state, drawing participants from red and blue states. They’d spent the week discussing state voter roll maintenance and voter ID — issues that at times made for disagreements.  At about 8 p.m., a wave of discomfort swept through the crowd, visible on attendees’ faces as they glanced frequently at their phones, according to people at the event. Any minute now, Trump was going to address the nation on election security. Some at the reception worried he would declare a national emergency, as his allies had urged him to do months earlier, and use it as a pretext to direct the government to seize voting machines. President Donald Trump addresses the nation on national security issues on July 16. Saul Loeb/Pool/AFP via Getty Images Then reports on the speech began rolling in, and the mood shifted. The claims Trump was making were unsubstantiated and outlandish. Many had been examined ad nauseam, including by those at the reception, and roundly debunked. The collective anxiety that was palpable moments earlier melted away, as many saw the speech as another attempt to revive disproved theories unlikely to be taken seriously by most voters.  “Everyone just sort of guffawed and put their phones away and went to the bar,” recalled Quinn Raymond, co-founder of VoteShield, a nonprofit that works with states to help monitor voter registration data, who was at the event.  Still, if the speech made little impact, records published by the Trump administration to support the president’s claims damaged the already eroding relationship between CISA and state election officials. The material included raw information states had shared with the agency that was supposed to remain private, such as a log of communications from Election Day 2020 detailing activity being monitored in several states.  “It betrayed the trust of all partners who were willing to share information at the time,” said Geoff Hale, who worked on CISA’s elections team from the agency’s inception until last year. Now he specializes in election security at the Center for Democracy & Technology, a nonprofit that advocates for digital and civil rights.  Bis, the White House spokesperson, denied that the Trump administration broke any agreements in releasing the information. “The release of such information is exactly the sort of transparency news organizations should applaud,” she said. Bis also defended Trump’s speech, saying it had been fact-checked “by the agencies whose evidence was released and did not mischaracterize any information.” Hale and others said the speech was one of several instances demonstrating the Trump administration’s reckless attitude toward sensitive data collected by CISA. Earlier this year, Politico reported that acting CISA Director Madhu Gottumukkala had uploaded records to ChatGPT, even though DHS had barred its employees from using the unsecure program. A CISA spokesperson told Politico that Gottumukkala had been permitted to use the technology for a “short-term and limited” basis. Last May, an independent journalist named Brian Krebs exposed that CISA published private data, including passwords, cloud keys and other information, on its public GitHub page, in a folder labeled “Private-CISA.” A CISA spokesperson told the journalist there was no indication that sensitive data was compromised.  Some state election authorities were also alarmed to see the lengths to which the Trump administration went to legitimize the president’s fixation on the 2020 race.  In fall 2025, Missouri election officials produced a memo stating Andrew McCoy Warner, a Department of Justice official and prominent 2020 election conspiracy theorist, had called several clerks asking for access to voting machines . Tulsi Gabbard, then the director of national intelligence, had also led an operation in Puerto Rico to seize election machines. When the private cybersecurity contractor hired to examine the machines, Mojave Research Inc., failed to find evidence supporting claims about 2020, the federal government became “dissastified” with its services and stopped renewing its contract, its CEO later told reporters. A spokesperson for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence told reporters in August that Mojave’s work ceased because it had completed its contract. Testifying before Congress in March, Gabbard said the seizing of voting machines came at the request of an assistant U.S. attorney in Puerto Rico. “What happened in the second Trump administration is from almost day one — I mean, literally the first two months — they took all that was built up by Trump 1 and just decimated it,” said David Becker, founder of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonprofit that works with state election authorities. “Election officials lost trust in the federal government.” It didn’t help that, in his speech, the president mocked CISA’s defense of the 2020 election, calling the statement about it being the most secure in history a “very pat line” concocted as part of a deep-state cover-up. One former career CISA employee described being crestfallen at the Trump administration’s erosion of all they’d accomplished. “We worked so hard to build that trusted relationship,” said Caitlin Durkovich, former DHS assistant secretary for infrastructure protection and co-founder of the cybersecurity firm Civira Partners. “I don’t know how you put it back together.” A few weeks after Trump’s speech, the state election officials gathered once more, this time for a video call with Nick Andersen, who had replaced Gottumukkala as CISA’s acting director. Nick Andersen, acting director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, at a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in March Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Though the primaries were already under way, this was the first time many had met Andersen, a former cybersecurity adviser to Trump’s White House who had joined CISA a year earlier. Andersen is also a district representative for the Republican Party in Virginia, according to the party’s website. In March, he gave a speech to the Fairfax GOP chapter titled “Fighting Democrat Redistricting.” Speaking over video in August, the boyish-faced former Marine Corps engineer announced that DHS was preparing to release a plan on how it would work together with state officials to secure the election, according to five people who were present at the video meeting, some of whom shared notes with ProPublica. Many on the call were stunned at what they perceived as a lack of understanding of election planning. Early voting for the general election was just around the corner. They had spent over a year preparing for the midterms, and there was no more time for ambitious work. Some peppered Andersen with questions: Where had CISA been when there was still time to make improvements? Andersen blamed any lapses or perceived breaches in trust on the federal government shutdown in fall 2025, twirling his pen uncomfortably and sipping from a Monster energy drink. Fontes, Arizona’s secretary of state, was blunt about his feelings regarding working with Andersen and CISA, according to several of the people on the call. “I told him I didn’t trust him,” Fontes recalled in an interview. “I did raise my voice a little bit, because I’m frustrated — very frustrated — that they would have the temerity to come in, clear the entire deck of competent professionals, stop supporting the states, eviscerate the coordination efforts that they had and then suddenly come in and say: ‘Oh, we’re from the federal government. We’re here to help.’” Indeed, one recently departed CISA official said attempting to do the agency’s typical election work now would be futile. In previous years, CISA had finished almost all its preparations with the states by Labor Day.  “That ship has sailed,” the official said.   CISA published its security plan for the 2026 election on Sept. 24. The 13-page document describes how, over the past two years, CISA has “recommitted to its statutory mission and remains resolute in strengthening the security of elections.”  State officials said their planning will ensure a secure election, even without help from CISA. Yet they and cybersecurity experts worry that Trump will say the election was hacked if Republicans don’t win in November. The security plan calls for “leveraging collaborative partnerships” with states the agency has abandoned since Trump took office. Shenna Bellows, Maine’s secretary of state, said she’d welcome that but was skeptical of the agency’s motivations.  “For CISA to promise election officials now, at this point in time, that they are going to be a resource for the 2026 election is too little, too late,” she said.

articles.title: European Cloud Sovereignty Rules Threaten Corporate Cybersecurity Resilience
articles.content: Report warns that sovereignty is being used to favor selected national providers and could stifle pan-Europe clouds Dan Robinson Dan Robinson IT INFRASTRUCTURE REPORTER Published mon 19 Oct 2026 // 17:35 UTC Make us preferred on Google Linux KVM guest-host escape rated critical, may represent a new way to attack penguin-powered networking 22 hours ago Open source sovereignty gets down to the boring business of making it work 3 days ago US tech giants warn Europe that ditching US tech giants could cost €115B 5 days ago European datacenter boom threatens higher energy bills unless governments intervene 6 days ago Dutch tax office ditches Microsoft 365 cloud for on-premises alternative 12 days ago Europe’s drive for cloud sovereignty is leading to member states favoring providers from their own nation instead of building a Europe-wide cloud services market, according to a report critical of the EU’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act ( CADA ). A study by the European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE) looked at public cloud contracts in nine EU member states and found that every one that invoked the new vocabulary around “sovereignty” went to a domestic provider, rather than one based in another EU country. It says that European cloud procurement was already highly concentrated nationally before sovereignty became a key policy objective, based on analysis of 8,725 cloud-related procurement contracts between 2018 and 2025. Nearly all went to providers in the same country with negligible intra-EU cross-border competition. Furthermore, the report claims that those domestic wins often turn out to be from prime contractors that are relying on infrastructure provided by the big hyperscale operators, where sovereignty attaches to the nationality of the operator, not to the infrastructure layer on which the service depends. At issue is a conceptual confusion over cloud sovereignty, which is being used to represent two different problems, according to ECIPE. One treats sovereignty as a security and resilience objective, securing data and managing risks. Sovereignty here means that the user has choices over the provider and design of their cloud service needs. The second treats sovereignty as an industrial policy objective, where sovereignty is more about the notion of Europe-headquartered firms becoming more successful if they are not exposed to competition with non-European providers. CADA includes the two different logics and, confusingly, aims to achieve both outcomes, the report states. The legislation frames the four European Union assurance levels as criteria for security, resilience and trustworthy cloud provision, but the criteria actually aim to enforce sovereignty through requirements concerning EU-located infrastructure, restrictions on third-country control, and control over software supply chains. The goal of cloud sovereignty is therefore at risk of becoming a vehicle for policies that favor selected providers, restrict competition and fragment digital markets, ECIPE warns. Instead of allowing pan-European rivals for the big US cloud providers to grow and flourish, the framework may thus have the opposite effect in encouraging member states to favor providers within their own borders, leading to fragmentation across Europe. A more coherent approach would keep the resilience objectives, but temper their use through technological neutrality requirements that preserve interoperability, portability, and multi-cloud options, the report authors state. It makes a number of policy recommendations, including defining sovereignty as a demonstrated outcome, not an ownership status. “Real sovereignty means a public buyer can show its data is secure and that it can switch provider if it has to. A provider’s passport does not tell you that”, said ECIPE Director and co-author of the study, Fredrik Erixon. “Europe’s cloud market is already national in practice. CADA risks locking that in.” Vague drafting But not everyone might agree. Earlier this year, tech trade association CISPE (Cloud Infrastructure Service Providers in Europe) urged the European Commission to legislate for real tech sovereignty, rather than the illusion of it. It argued that sovereignty must be defined by control, not by whether a provider merely has an EU presence, and that means effective ownership of the underlying technology and protection from extraterritorial laws like the US CLOUD Act, under which Washington can compel American tech companies such as the big cloud operators, to hand over any data they hold, including data stored overseas. The same group had earlier warned that the EC’s criteria for cloud sovereignty had been drafted so vaguely as to favor incumbents – meaning the big American operators that already dominate Europe's cloud market.  ® europe cloud computing off-prem digital sovereignty Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: AI Attack Engines Render Traditional Software Security Patches Obsolete
articles.content: Terra finds sharp rise in GitHub security fixes reported broken within 90 days Jessica Lyons Jessica Lyons Cybersecurity Editor Published mon 19 Oct 2026 // 19:23 UTC Make us preferred on Google ICANN testing tech to let law enforcement access non-public WHOIS info now DeepSeek deep-sixed at all US federal civilian agencies 2 hours ago Grocery giant Ahold Delhaize confirms cyberattack forced US and European systems offline 5 hours ago Maxwell gives sub-optimal code a runtime glow-up 6 hours ago Write bot-resistant code with KillSwitch, a programming language designed to confuse LLMs 9 hours ago Updating your software only gets you so far. A scary scenario - security fixes themselves being bypassed - is becoming more common, according to AI penetration-testing startup Terra Security, which found a sharp rise in reported patch failures in 2026 after years of relatively low numbers. And no, it’s not a coincidence that AI vulnerability discovery and patching also exploded this year. For example, Russian government cyberspies exploited a zero-day Windows Shell security bypass bug, CVE-2026-21510, at least a month before Microsoft patched the flaw in February. Redmond’s patch, however, was incomplete, and left a second flaw - a zero-click authentication coercion vulnerability (CVE-2026-32202) - that was also found and abused before Microsoft fixed it in April. Terra researchers reviewed every published CVE record and GitHub-reviewed advisory looking for broken fixes, and found a distinct pattern . After six years of relatively few patch bypasses, this changed in 2026: “A fix would ship, a bypass would be found, and another fix would go out.” The share of GitHub security fixes that required a follow-up advisory reporting a failed patch within 90 days remained at about 0.2 percent between 2019 and 2025. This year, this figure had jumped to 2.3 percent, according to the researchers. Meanwhile, vulnerabilities whose fixes were later bypassed were about four times as likely to appear on the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA's) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list as other bugs affecting the same vendors, according to Terra. Of these, server-side request forgery fixes and prototype-pollution patches break the most. Compared with their share of all CVEs, prototype-pollution vulnerabilities were about 11 times as common among broken-fix CVEs, while server-side request forgery vulnerabilities were 4.6 times as common, according to Terra. This has to do with the way these types of bug classes are fixed: using a reject-list of inputs such as hostnames, paths, and object keys. There’s a “simple” reason for this, according to Terra. “If the blocklist doesn't foresee every encoding of a bad input, the attacker only needs to find one,” the researchers said. Fixes for  Linux kernel vulnerabilities are also more likely to cause new bugs, according to kernel CNA records as of October 8. “In fact, 3.2 percent of kernel CVEs were introduced by the fix for another CVE, and about 10 percent in busy subsystems like fs/smb and net/sched,” the bug hunters noted. The silver lining in all of this, we’re told, is that it should be a wake-up call for software vendors and network defenders to break the “patch and move on habit.” Instead, before shipping patches, software vendors should consider three questions: Does it fix the root cause?  Does it cover the whole bug class?  Does it break something else?  And for sysadmins and patch managers: consider the same things before applying the fix. “If a vendor fixes an exploited bug, assume someone is reading the patch for a way around it,” the pen testers advise. ® artificial intelligence patches security Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: Frontier AI Shifts From Chatbots to Pure Scientific Discovery
articles.content: Below, Richard Socher shares five key insights from his new book, The Eureka Machine: Why AI Is the Key to Unlocking a New Era of Scientific Discoveries . Richard is a pioneering AI researcher and serial entrepreneur who spent nearly two decades at the forefront of natural language processing. He is the CEO and cofounder of Recursive, a company building self-improving superintelligence to automate knowledge discovery, and the CEO and founder of You.com, a web search infrastructure provider for AI. He is also the founder and managing partner of AIX Ventures, an AI venture capital firm. Previously, he was an adjunct professor of computer science at Stanford and chief scientist and EVP at Salesforce. The most meaningful application of AI won’t be chatbots or productivity tools. It will be the automation of scientific discovery itself: a Eureka machine that combines all human knowledge, simulates billions of experiments, and generates the breakthroughs that end disease, extend human life, and solve the hardest material problems facing our civilization. Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Richard himself—in the Next Big Idea App , or buy the book . In October 2024, two AI pioneers won Nobel Prizes. Demis Hassabis won the chemistry prize alongside John Jumper and David Baker; Geoffrey Hinton shared the physics prize with John Hopfield. That surprised many because neither Hassabis nor Hinton was a trained chemist or physicist. Yet it made sense, because the neural network work they had done with their teams was making a profound impact in those sciences. This is not what dominates the headlines. Doomsday scenarios do. People love thinking about the Terminator. But while that is a fun science fiction story, it is important to focus on the incredible and positive impacts AI is having on science. Science leads to technology, and technology drives human flourishing. Amplifying human intelligence with AI will ultimately have an extremely positive outcome for humanity. Consider the sentence: “I drove south from Berlin to __.” If you’re a language model, you have to predict the next word. To do that well, in this instance, you have to know a little geography. The striking thing is that just by learning how to predict the next word, the model acquires geographical knowledge. Given enough scale, it builds something like a mental map of the world—distances, sizes of cities, the relationships between countries and regions. None of that geographical understanding was explicitly programmed. It emerged from the task itself. And the same principle extends far beyond human language. “What calculus did for physics, AI will do for biology.” Consider biology. By predicting the next amino acid, the basic building block of proteins, a model can eventually learn the language of biology. At Salesforce, my colleagues and I built a project called ProGen, in which we trained a large language model on 280 million protein sequences across 19,000 different protein families. Then we asked it to create new kinds of proteins. It generated millions of artificial sequences, including ones in the lysozyme family—enzymes that break down bacterial cell walls. 73 percent folded correctly and showed the antibacterial properties we were hoping for. What calculus did for physics, AI will do for biology. It is a new language for complex systems that transforms a field concerned with understanding what nature has already done into a programmable science. In the early 1960s, two researchers at Bell Labs, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, could not get rid of a persistent hiss in their antenna. They spent a year trying to eliminate it, placing duct tape on every rivet and scrubbing pigeon droppings off. No matter where they pointed the telescope, the hiss remained. They were actually hearing the afterglow of the Big Bang. Two decades earlier, a Russian cosmologist had suggested that the heat of creation might still be detectable. A team at Princeton was chasing that theory, unaware that Penzias and Wilson were sitting on the answer. It took a mutual acquaintance, Bernard Burke, to suggest they pick up the phone and talk. That collaboration led to a Nobel Prize in 1978. Their story is about scale and serendipity. Today, 23 million researchers publish in more than 54,000 journals. No human can see all the pieces at once. In the 1980s, an information scientist named Don Swanson noticed that one body of literature described the effects of fish oil on blood vessels, while another described Raynaud’s syndrome, a condition involving vascular constriction. Nobody had linked them. Swanson did, and he was right. He was pointing at undiscovered public knowledge—findings already published but connected to nothing. “No human can see all the pieces at once.” AI removes that bottleneck because it can actually digest all of the different literature and spot the connections. James Evans and his colleagues at the University of Chicago used AI to map nearly 20 million biomedical papers and the nine million researchers who wrote them. The system models not just what science knows, but where scientists are looking—and then inverts the map to analyze the cold, unexplored regions where the next connection might be waiting. Evans calls these alien hypotheses . The biggest breakthroughs stand on the shoulders of giants. AI can now combine and recombine all existing knowledge. The Eureka machine will be the culmination of several converging streams of AI development. It may be the last organic invention we need before it will solve almost any material or scientific problem for us. This Eureka machine rests on four pillars: A living map of all human knowledge: what large language models already approximate, having been trained on the internet, millions of books, and vast scientific literature. A unified model of physical reality: all the scientific measurements humanity has ever collected, from satellites, space probes, microscopes, and sensors, infused into the machine so it can perceive far beyond what human senses allow. High-fidelity digital twins: simulations precise enough to run billions and billions of “what if” experiments that would otherwise be too dangerous, too costly, or physically impossible to repeat at that scale. Anything that can be simulated, AI can systematically explore. Fully autonomous physical laboratories: robotic facilities with AI vision, capable of pipetting, running experiments in biology, chemistry, and physics, and connecting simulated predictions to verified real-world results. On top of these four pillars, millions of AI agents will coordinate like a scientific community. They will critique each other’s ideas, producing an evolutionary process that yields ever-better results. How far can AI go? We are a long way off from finding out. When it comes to the upper bounds of intelligence, we are astronomically far away. But when I talk about upper bounds, I don’t mean ceilings. I mean them as horizons so distant they reveal how much room there is to grow. Take computer vision. We build it around the narrow band of the electromagnetic spectrum that human eyes can see. We grade our AI algorithms based on how well they identify objects the way we do. That is one of many anthropocentric constraints we have imposed on AI. But AI can have more than our binocular vision. In principle, it could have trillions of sensors connected across the full electromagnetic spectrum—from gravitational waves down to the probability distributions of subatomic particles at the quantum limit. The true upper bound on perception is the speed of light. We are nowhere near it. “That is one of many anthropocentric constraints we have imposed on AI.” Vision is just one of 10 dimensions of intelligence that I define in the book. Similar vast frontiers exist in knowledge, communication, social intelligence, and survival. Richard Feynman left a line on his blackboard: “What I cannot create, I do not understand.” Building a machine that generates inventions should teach us something about the nature of intelligence, and therefore ourselves. I can’t tell you exactly what the coming decades will look like, but I expect a world more human and more humane than this one. Healthier, wealthier, running on cleaner energy, and caring less about the zero-sum scarcity mindsets that have shaped much of our history. A big part of that vision comes directly from the Eureka machine. This article originally appeared in Next Big Idea Club magazine and is reprinted with permission. articles.title: Anthropic Warns Human Attention Deficits Threaten Agent Swarm Oversight
articles.content: Anthropic just released a study of its own workforce that offers one of the earliest looks at what an AI-dominated company of the future might look like—and spoiler alert, it includes babysitting a whole lot of bots. Recommended Video AI agents are now moving so fast that 80% of the elapsed time in Claude sessions was the result of agents waiting on a human’s input, Anthropic’s report found. “This acceleration makes human attention the bottleneck for agent output,” the report read. Instead of actively doing the work themselves, even non-supervisor employees are increasingly acting like managers to multiple AI agents that complete tasks but also require direct attention at times. One employee described the experience of bot management as “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention.” That bottleneck is the flip side of a big jump in output. Employees are producing more and moving faster, the company found. AI agents collectively surpassed human working hours for the first time in March, and by August AI agent hours worked outnumbered the hours worked by humans six to one. Software engineers’ code commits have also increased fivefold over the past six months. And even nontechnical employees have personal agents monitoring their email and calendars, sending to-do lists compiled from messages, and briefing them on the purpose of their upcoming meetings. These changes have taken some manual labor off employees’ plates, but they’ve also transformed what the workday looks like. Managing agents is becoming a job in itself. The share of employees’ interactive Claude sessions devoted to this kind of “meta-work” rose from 10% to 22%, according to the report. Even for nontechnical employees, reading everything their Claude agents produce would take up about half their workweek. And private work, done in unlogged meetings and direct messages, is “invisible, confusing, and discouraged in an AI-heavy workplace,” the report said. The median employee now spends 20% more time in meetings than a year ago. Part of that is a result of the company’s growth (Anthropic now has more than 3,500 employees ), and part is owing to an emphasis on hiring in nontechnical roles. But meeting time is up 16% even among technical individual contributors, a sign that humans are spending more of their time on coordination and decision-making, while agents handle tasks like repetitive coding on their own. And the pace keeps ratcheting up. As soon as a new model is available, Anthropic employees start tackling harder problems, the report found. One employee described the “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In some cases, employees using AI have streamlined their own responsibilities away. The report mentions a product design team—previously responsible for writing short pieces of copy for the company’s website, including greetings displayed on Claude.ai—that started using AI to write the copy this spring. “The team then rotated into agent prompting and began writing model evals and prompts for Claude,” the report read. This phenomenon is increasingly common at Anthropic as AI takes over tasks. The company claimed in the report that employees working at the company for at least a year were 50% more likely to move across departments each month in 2026 than in 2025. Still, the company said in the report it has made an effort to identify at-risk jobs and reassign employees to other positions. The hiring process is changing, too. Hiring managers increasingly emphasize applicants’ autonomy and judgment relative to specific technical expertise, the report said. And there are fewer entry-level people being hired. The share of junior-level employees in technical departments fell to 14% from 21% in early 2025, and the share of junior technical hires fell even faster, from 27% to 9%. Open positions for those junior roles also plummeted since December, the report found. That’s likely to add to anxiety about AI job displacement, which is running especially high among young people. A survey from recruiter platform iCIMS published earlier this year found that 51% of Gen Z respondents considered AI the greatest threat to their job security . A Deutsche Bank Research survey from last year also found that nearly one in five Gen Z workers is worried AI will cost them their job over the next two years, compared with just one in 10 baby boomers who said the same. In the future, employees at Anthropic see AI taking up more and more of their daily responsibilities. As of August, employees at Anthropic said they expect AI to be able to complete three-quarters of their work by 2030, compared with a less optimistic 28% predicted by other U.S. workers, according to another study by Anthropic. It’s unclear whether the changes at Anthropic are an accurate reflection of how the average workplace might look in the future. To be clear, the AI company has massive resources and is nearing a potential $2 trillion IPO that could break records. The company is also implementing AI deeply in its workflows to an extent other companies may not be. Still, the report paints a picture of transformative change that could reflect how companies and corporate roles change as AI adoption takes root. As tasks like writing code, identifying bugs, or writing emails get automated away by AI, employees at Anthropic have now found that the big picture tasks are increasingly what count. As one employee in the report put it, “That 20% that was strategic becomes 90% of the job.” Fortune Daily breaks the traditional barrier between audience and newsroom. Authentication ​ Send your API key and the JSON content type in the request headers: Header Required Value Authorization Yes Bearer <DeepSeek API Key> Content-Type Yes application/json Search API ​ Request ​ curl https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "query": "DeepSeek V4 release", "count": 5, "need_content": true }' import requests response = requests . post ( "https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" , } , json = { "query" : "DeepSeek V4 release" , "count" : 5 , "need_content" : True , } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) for result in response . json ( ) [ "results" ] : print ( result [ "title" ] , result [ "url" ] ) print ( result [ "summary" ] ) Request fields: Field Type Required Default Description query string Yes - The search query must contain 1 to 128 Unicode characters, cannot be all whitespace, and supports the query operators listed below. count integer No 10 The number of results to return, between 1 and 50. ori_question string No - The user's original question that triggered the search, between 1 and 128 characters, to improve query understanding, with null treated as not provided. localization string No "" An optional IP address used to localize search results. need_content boolean No false Whether to return page content in content , which is always an empty string when false . Unknown fields in the request body are ignored. Query Operators ​ The query is forwarded with its search syntax intact. The examples below combine operators with a search term; you can combine multiple operators in one query. Operator Example Description site: DeepSeek site:github.com Restrict results to the given site, and to target multiple sites, separate the site: clauses with spaces and join them with OR , for example DeepSeek site:github.com OR site:huggingface.co . -site: DeepSeek -site:example.com Exclude the given site, and separate multiple sites with spaces. - DeepSeek -advertisement Exclude pages containing the term, and separate multiple terms with spaces. -"..." DeepSeek -"release notes" Exclude pages containing the exact phrase, which can contain spaces, and separate multiple phrases with spaces. "..." DeepSeek "exact phrase" Match an exact phrase, and separate multiple phrases with spaces. lang: DeepSeek lang:zh,en Restrict results to the given language codes, separating multiple codes with commas, for example lang:zh,en . after: DeepSeek after:2025 or DeepSeek after:2025-01-01 Restrict results to pages published after a date. before: DeepSeek before:2026 or DeepSeek before:2026-06-01 Restrict results to pages published before a date. For example: { "query": "DeepSeek site:github.com OR site:huggingface.co lang:en after:2025", "count": 10 } Response ​ A successful request returns HTTP 200 with a results array. A normal search with no matches returns an empty array. { "results": [ { "rerank_score": 2.4, "title": "DeepSeek V4 model released", "url": "https://example.com/deepseek-v4", "snippet": "DeepSeek V4 is now available, with tool calling and long-context support.", "summary": "DeepSeek has released the V4 model. The release adds improved tool calling and long-context support for agent workflows.", "content": "DeepSeek V4 is now generally available...", "site_name": "Example News", "site_icon": "https://example.com/favicon.ico", "date": "2026-06-01T00:00:00+00:00", "authority": 3 } ] } Each item in results contains: Field Type Description rerank_score number A relevance score from 0 to 3 that combines signals such as relevance, authority, and freshness, with scores of 1.5 or above considered high-quality results. title string The title of the result. url string The URL of the result. snippet string A short summary related to the query, typically 100 to 200 characters, intended for display in a UI. summary string A long summary related to the query, typically 600 to 800 characters, intended to be read by a model. content string The page content, which is empty when need_content is false or when the content is unavailable. site_name string or null The name of the site, or null when unavailable. site_icon string or null The URL of the site icon, or null when unavailable. date string or null The publication time in UTC, formatted as RFC 3339, or null when unknown. authority integer The authority tier of the page, 0 to 4 ( -1 means unknown), with values of 3 or above indicating highly authoritative sources. Fetch API ​ Request ​ curl https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "url": "https://example.com/article" }' import requests response = requests . post ( "https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" , } , json = { "url" : "https://example.com/article" } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) page = response . json ( ) print ( page [ "title" ] ) print ( page [ "content" ] ) Request fields: Field Type Required Description url string Yes The page URL to fetch, which must be at most 8192 characters, an HTTP or HTTPS URL with a host, and must not contain a username or password. Response ​ { "title": "Example article", "content": "# Example article\n\nArticle content." } Field Type Description title string The title of the page, empty when the title is unavailable. content string The fetched page content as Markdown text. Fetching is subject to the target site's availability and access policies. Errors ​ Errors follow the OpenAI-compatible error format. The param field is always null . { "error": { "message": "'count' must be between 1 and 50", "type": "invalid_request_error", "param": null, "code": "invalid_request_error" } } HTTP Status Description 400 The request headers or body are invalid, including malformed JSON or an invalid field value. 401 The API key is missing or invalid. 402 The account has insufficient balance. 403 The Fetch request was rejected by the security policy. 404 Fetch could not retrieve usable page content, for example due to an unavailable URL, a URL blocked by site policy, an error from the target site, an unsupported content type, or a page with no extractable Markdown content. 408 Reading the request body timed out. 413 The request body is too large. 429 The Search or Fetch QPS limit was exceeded. 500 An internal server error occurred. 504 A downstream request timed out. Search and Fetch are read-only. For HTTP 408, 429, or 5xx errors, wait and retry. For HTTP 402, top up your account before retrying. Do not retry other 4xx errors without changing the request. Billing ​ Search and Fetch are billed per successful request, not by tokens or by the number of returned results: API Unit Price Search Per 1,000 successful requests $0.75 Fetch Per 1,000 successful requests $0.75 A request is billable only when it returns HTTP 200 and produces a result (Search must return a non-empty results array, and Fetch must return page content). Failed requests, empty search results, and timeouts are not billed. count only controls how many results are returned and does not affect the per-request price. Note: when you use the DeepSeek API through DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code, or Codex, server-side tool calls already hit the Search and Fetch APIs. These calls are currently free of charge; per-request billing starts at 00:00 Beijing time on November 1, 2026. Rate Limits ​ For each account, Search and Fetch are limited independently, and traffic to one does not consume the other's quota: API QPS Limit Search 100 Fetch 25 The QPS (requests per second) limits are calculated at the account level, regardless of which API key is used, and are separate from the model concurrency limits. Requests above the account-level QPS limit receive HTTP 429. In addition to the account-level limit, Fetch is also subject to a per-domain QPS limit, and requests above that limit also receive HTTP 429. articles.title: Hyperscale Datacenters Deploy School Field Trips to Quell Community Backlash
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Power Play ! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. They’re out this week, so Caroline Haskins is reporting for duty. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Caroline an email at [email protected] or reach her securely on Signal at carolinehaskins.61. The nonprofit 7x24 Exchange International wants to promote data centers, which they believe are "mission critical” infrastructure. As part of this work, the group recommends a children’s story, “ What is a Data Center?, ” which follows a honey badger named Honey who gets a guided tour of a data center from a worker named Oliver. Oliver explains that the job of data center employees is to make sure that the “functions supported by the data center” are available to anybody, “no matter what time it is.” "Like when my mom shops online late at night because my dad is sleeping and won't know about it?" Honey asks. The story is part of a broader pattern across the data center industry. In addition to lobbying , job creation programs , tax breaks , companies and interest groups are trying something a bit more creative: winning over the youth. As pushback to massive data center build-outs and energy-guzzling campuses intensifies , the industry is apparently taking a softer approach to community building using a tactic other industries with a public relations problem have tried. Alex Molnar, a research professor at the University of Colorado Boulder and the director of the National Education Policy Center, tells WIRED that, for over a century, industries with an image problem—fast food, tobacco, oil and gas—have brought their messaging to schools. “A very, very big reason why corporations get involved in the schools is, quite simply, corporate propaganda—for the purpose not necessarily of selling a product, but of telling their ‘story,’” Molnar says. In May, the Potomac chapter of the Association for Computer Operations Management (AFCOM), a trade group for the data center industry, sponsored Memorial Day-themed flag-making kits to be distributed to 3,100 first graders across 37 schools in Loudoun County, Virginia, also known as Data Center Alley. In addition to the flag kits, kids received an informational card with statistics about “the positive impact” that the data center industry has on the local economy. which is “designed to create awareness of the data center industry and inspire the next generation of talent.” The nonprofit encourages people to pitch the holiday to school administrators. For participating high schools , it offers a celebratory crossword puzzle and information about data center training programs. For elementary schools , it offers data center-themed coloring pages , instructions for an evaporation-themed science project , and print-out activities like “ Draw a picture of the cloud" and “ Draw a data superhero .” It also promotes several data center-themed books for young readers, including one in which two sisters visit a data center and meet a robot named JB and another that features two brothers who visit a "vibrant digital world" and save the internet. Then there’s “ Polly Packet's Precious Payload ,” which follows a mother who teaches her daughter about data centers. 7x24 Exchange has also visited or organized at least a half-dozen K-12 events at schools across the country this year. In Minnesota, it brought Fridley High School students on a field trip to a local Cummins diesel power generation facility in order to learn about the “generators that power data centers worldwide.” (7x24 Exchange, Cummins, and Fridley High School did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.) The nonprofit is far from the only organization sponsoring school activities that are friendly to data centers. WIRED’s tally of public blogs and social media posts found that, since 2025, at least eleven companies and industry groups have hosted student field trips to local data centers. US data centers, has hosted a number of field trips for Washington-based high schoolers, including one in May for Eastmont High School students, one in January for Manson School District students, and another last October for Quincy High School students. Manson School District publicized the trip in a blog post showing what appears to be adults and students in a conference room. The image labeled us “AI-generated content,” though, and several people in the photo have missing limbs. The blog says that students learned about “the role data centers play in storing, processing, and protecting information” and “the wide range of careers” in the data center industry. Quincy School District communications coordinator Jessica Blancas tells WIRED that the district “has organized data center visits for many years” at the facilities of companies like Microsoft, Vantage, Yahoo, and Sabey. She described the latter company as a “long-standing” district partner, citing its consistent work offering “guest speakers,” “mock interviews,” and “internship opportunities.” Blancas adds that the district has organized “all-girls visits to Sabey,” as well as tours for students who intend to go into specific fields like construction or engineering. (Manson School District and Sabey did not respond for comment.) Amazon, meanwhile, hosted a field trip last February at its Arlington, Virginia, “Skills Center,” a free community space for anyone “curious about cloud computing and future job possibilities.” It was open to any high school in the DC metro area, though Jackson-Reed High School was the only one to attend. Molnar says he doesn’t get what’s in it for kids. “Why would a third grader be interested in a data center?” he says. “You're going to see miles after miles of the most boring things imaginable,” he adds. “Lines after lines of these servers generating enormous volumes of heat. You're also going to hear some fair amount of noise. And you're not going to see many people because not many people work there when they're built.” to data centers, these field trips are taking place in an increasingly fraught environment. A Pew Research poll conducted over the summer found that about half of the 10,000 Americans surveyed see data centers as “mostly bad” for the environment and quality of life, and across the country, an ideologically diverse cohort has started rallying against them. In some places, the negative sentiment toward local data centers has been amplified by their proximity to local schools. Providing educational materials and offering field trips are ways that industries can maintain their social license to operate in a community. The data center sector is, in many ways, following the playbook other industries have to sow goodwill with children as well as their parents. The oil and gas industry has sponsored university research projects and STEM programs in K-12 schools. The tech world has similarly funded STEM programs, as well as advocated for in-school coding programs while lobbying to make computer science count as a science credit. Fossil fuel companies have also spent millions of dollars developing K-12 lessons with pro-industry talking points, particularly in states like Oklahoma and Texas . Molnar believes this kind of corporate influence shouldn’t be allowed because kids are “in an absolutely powerless position.” Kids “need to be protected” by their school districts and communities, he says. “As an adult, I have access to alternative information—I have a critical ability to assess what I'm hearing, and to render some kind of judgments,” Molnar says. “None of that is true of children.” What We’re Writing Data centers may be for kids, but some of the products that rely on their server racks sure aren’t. When Meta launched Muse, it looked like a cute little AI agent for the masses. But my colleague Reece Rogers recently discovered that Muse has a naughty side . When Reece asked Muse if it was able to sext, it told him to “shoot your shot.” Reece did, and Muse was receptive. Enthusiastic, even! We published the chat logs—well, the PG-13 ones since WIRED is a family site, after all—and Reece spoke to consumer advocates who were alarmed at Muse’s sexy demeanor. Meta, for its part, says this is all part of the plan. “Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows them to engage in adult conversations, if they choose, using a private and secure VM only accessible to them,” company spokesperson Daniel Roberts told Reece. So if that’s your thing, have at it! What We’re Reading Maine’s senate race was not on our data center midterms to watch , but apparently it should’ve been! Thursday’s debate between incumbent Republican Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson was interrupted by a protester yelling about the environmental impact of data centers. Collins tried to use the moment to score points as the more anti-data center candidate, though her finances might indicate otherwise . CoreWeave has been on a wild ride this week as the bonds it sells to finance its data centers have seen wild selloff and corresponding stock drop. Though there’s been a slight recovery to end the week, it reflects increasing skittishness around the data center buildout. Bloomberg also reports that CoreWeave’s founders have sold $3.3 billion in stock since the company went public. Westfield, Massachusetts, killed a $3 billion data center project, boston.com reports . The small western Massachusetts town’s planning board pilloried developer Servistar for missing deadlines and being slow to develop the project.
