articles.title: Fundamental Physics Constraints Threaten Exponential Expansion of AI Compute Clusters
articles.content: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” on how we might manipulate and control things on an extremely small scale. There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued, or from storing every book ever written in something the size of a dust speck—or, ultimately, from arranging matter atom by atom. Biology already did versions of this (a living cell keeps its instructions in a wisp of DNA), so all of this was plainly permitted by the laws of physics. We simply had not built the tools yet. In other words, there was plenty of room at the bottom. He was right, and for decades we descended into that space almost for free. The transistor—the switch at the heart of computer chips—repeatedly halved in size so that chips doubled in density; a computer that once filled a room now fits inside a watch. But that easy descent has now stalled, and the clearest sign is the buildout of data centers. Six of the biggest hyperscalers, the companies that run the world’s largest such facilities, are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure, about twice the record they set in 2025, pouring concrete and copper and silicon into new sites faster than the electrical grid can feed them. That buildout buys performance by brute force, adding more of what we already know how to make. The other kind of progress, the kind that made computer chips better, is the one that is quietly running out. The trend lines that tracked the dramatic improvements of the 20th-century information age are now bending—or breaking—with the dawn of the 21st century’s intelligence age. Moore’s Law, which plots how densely transistors can be constructed on silicon, has slowed down; Dennard’s Law, which states that power consumption in a given patch of computer chip stays the same even as it gets more and more packed with smaller and smaller transistors, has ended; Koomey’s Law, which traces how much computation we can wring from each joule of energy, has begun to flag; Kryder’s Law, which describes how tightly bits can be packed to build magnetic storage, has slowed to a crawl; and Keck’s Law, which charts the exponential rise in the amount of information a single conventional optical fiber can carry, is flattening. But these scaling laws are merely observations about systems that we have engineered; they are not fundamental physical laws. The physical limits of computing and communications—dictated by quantum mechanics, general relativity, and information theory—lie far below anything in a data center today. The scaling laws chart the descent behind us. The fundamental physical limits chart the room that remains. Some of these limits may be far out of reach in practice. But they are still worth exploring, because the work pays twice: once in technology development and once in fundamental science. A proof-of-­concept system that approaches a limit is at once a technology that forces stalled paradigms to give way and an experiment that deepens our understanding of the physical laws themselves. During his 1959 lecture, Feynman offered two prizes of $1,000 each out of his own pocket. One would go to the first person to build a working electric motor smaller than a 0.4-millimeter cube. He expected the challenge to force someone to invent a genuinely new microtechnology. Instead, about a year later, a Caltech-trained engineer named William McLellan turned up with the motor built and running. The ­quarter-­milligram machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watch­maker’s lathe, under a microscope. Feynman, by his own account, was only slightly disappointed. The prize had proved his point in the least interesting way imaginable. The room really was down there, but reaching this first milestone had taken no new technology at all—just an unusually patient man with steady hands. The second prize aged differently, and more instructively. It was offered to whoever could shrink a page of text by a factor of 25,000 in each direction, small enough for the whole Britannica to fit on a pinhead. That one stood unclaimed for a quarter of a century. It was finally won in 1985 by Tom Newman, a Stanford graduate student who used an electron-beam lithography machine—an ancestor of pattern-making tools used in chipmaking today—to transcribe the opening page of A Tale of Two Cities at the required scale. The descent was already well underway, however. The year before Feynman’s talk, Jack Kilby, newly hired at Texas Instruments and with no vacation yet to take, spent that July nearly alone in the lab while his colleagues enjoyed time off, and by that September he had wired together a transistor, a capacitor, and three resistors, all made from a single sliver of germanium. This proved that an entire circuit could be carved from one block of semiconductor. The machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watch­maker’s lathe, under a microscope. The idea took off, and the number of components on a chip kept doubling on a schedule so regular that Gordon Moore, in a 1965 trade-magazine article, simply drew a line through the trend and extended it into the future. That line became Moore’s Law. Moore, though, never claimed transistors could shrink forever. He observed that at any given moment there is a certain number of components that makes each one of them as cheap as possible to manufacture. In 1965, that number was 50. Put in too few transistors and you waste the chip; cram in too many and manufacturing errors multiply and yields collapse. It was this cost-minimizing number that was doubling at a steady pace. Slowing down Many of the trend lines that measure improvements in computing and communications over time have been flattening. The most famous is Moore’s Law, which tracks transistor density on chips. The clearest slowdown has been in Dennard scaling, shown here as clock speed, which stopped climbing around 2004. In this plot, a straight line would represent a periodic doubling. The more horizontal the line becomes, the slower the doubling. SOURCES: STANFORD CPU DB; INTEL; APPLE; TECHINSIGHTS; KOOMEY ET AL.; COMPUTER HISTORY MUSEUM; IBM; TOSHIBA; SEAGATE; BELL SYSTEM TECHNICAL JOURNAL; OFC AND ECOC CONFERENCE PAPERS For four decades the descent came with another gift: Dennard scaling, so named for the IBM engineer Robert Dennard, who spelled it out in 1974. Each time transistors shrank, they also switched faster and drew proportionally less power, so every generation was an automatic win. Around 2004, though, the gift ran out. Chips could no longer shed the heat of running every transistor flat out; clock speeds, which had raced past three gigahertz, stopped climbing, and Intel canceled the four-gigahertz processor it had promised. The industry pivoted to packing multiple processing cores onto a chip rather than making one core faster, and the texture of progress changed. Progress is now bought mostly by scaling up the system—more chips wired together, more memory feeding them, more power and cooling around them—rather than by shrinking the transistor. This is most visible in AI, where training compute, the total count of arithmetic operations spent to train a model, has doubled roughly every six months since 2010, far faster than the pace of Moore’s Law allows. Little of that progress is due to shrinking. Computer chips still get better, and transistors still improve and get more densely packed, but each new generation arrives more slowly and pays back less in speed and power than the one before it. Nothing in that slowdown is a law of physics, though. The components of computing still sit far above their fundamental limits. Before we get to those limits, it is worth measuring how far the descent has already gone. In the nearly eight decades since the first transistor, the density of transistors on a chip has grown by 10 orders of magnitude—a 1 followed by 10 zeros, or a factor of 10 billion. Now more than 100 million transistors fit in a square millimeter (100 billion or more to a chip). Computational speed has grown even more, by 12 orders of magnitude, or a factor of a trillion; energy per operation has fallen 17 orders of magnitude, from about 100 joules for an early vacuum-tube machine down to a femto­joule—one-quadrillionth of a joule—for a single switch of a logic gate. These are not small improvements. But the floor, for computing performance, lies lower still. How much lower could we go? Around the turn of the millennium, the MIT physicist Seth Lloyd took the question to its extreme: Imagine an ordinary lump of matter, a kilogram of it—about the mass of a laptop—packed into a liter of space. How much computing could the laws of physics, pushed to their absolute limit, ever wring from that kilogram? In a 2000 paper in Nature titled “Ultimate physical limits to computation,” he worked out the answer and called the imaginary machine the ultimate laptop. The speed such a machine can achieve is governed by its energy. A kilogram of matter, according to E = mc 2 , holds about 9 ×10 16 joules, which is roughly what the entire United States draws from its electrical grid every two days. Spend all of that on computation, and the ultimate laptop runs at roughly 5 ×10 50 operations per second, some 35 orders of magnitude faster than a leading chip today. The catch is what running that quickly would look like. Concentrating a kilogram’s rest energy into pure computation would turn the machine into a plasma of about a billion degrees, a state closer to that of the universe in the first minutes after the Big Bang than anything we would recognize as a laptop. Such a machine is, to put it mildly, a very long way off. The next limit, which governs how much energy a computation must waste, is much closer, and companies are already pushing toward it. In 1961, Rolf Landauer, a physicist at IBM, showed that information and thermodynamics are bound together: Erasing a single bit must release a minimum quantity of heat, about 2.9 ×10 -21 joules at room temperature. The figure is small, yet a chip today spends several hundred thousand times more than that on every switch. Memory density obeys a limit of its own, and this one reaches all the way to gravity. How many bits can a region of space hold? In 1981, the physicist Jacob Bekenstein, while working out the thermodynamics of black holes, determined the amount: The information inside any bounded region is limited by its size and the energy it contains. For a region the size of Lloyd’s ultimate laptop, that comes to about 10 42 bits, some 10 36 to a cubic millimeter—nearly 30 orders of magnitude beyond what a device that size can store today. Approaching the limits Over the decades, we have pushed the performance of our computers and our communications technology closer and closer to fundamental limits. The biggest change has been in the energy required for a single computation, which has dropped by 17 orders of magnitude since the 1940s, a factor of a hundred thousand trillion. But even with that big drop, we’re still a factor of several hundred thousand from the fundamental physical limit, set by information theory and the laws of thermo­dynamics. The largest gap exists for computational speed: Our current chips are some 35 orders of magnitude—that’s a 1 followed by 35 zeros—short of what quantum mechanics allows for a one-kilogram computer. SOURCES: LLOYD (2000); BEKENSTEIN (1981); LANDAUER (1961); HOLEVO (1973); CAVES AND DRUMMOND (1994); BURKS (1947); BELL SYSTEM TECHNICAL JOURNAL; IEEE IRDS; NVIDIA; CISCO The last limit is on communication—how fast information can be moved. Every wire and every fiber ultimately carries its signal on quanta, the indivisible packets (photons in the case of light) in which energy travels. In 1973, the Soviet mathematician Alexander Holevo determined the ultimate limit on how much information a stream of quanta can convey. A watt of light delivers only so many photons each second, and quantum mechanics fixes how many distinguishable ways they can arrive—how many messages a receiver could ever tell apart. A single channel carrying one watt, at the Holevo limit, could deliver on the order of 10 17 bits per second. Today’s optical links, or interconnects, deliver about one-millionth that rate for the same power. But the gap is narrowing quickly inside data centers, where each generation of interconnects is asked to move more bits on less power, spending less energy on the electronics and using light to cover more of the distance. Four limits, then, mark the true bottom, and they derive from three of the most fundamental theories we have. Quantum mechanics sets how fast a machine can compute. General relativity caps how much it can remember. And information theory limits both how fast it can communicate and how little energy an irreversible step can cost. There is no road map to reaching these limits, and they hold whether or not anyone is trying. Measured against them, the descent has barely begun. The biggest of the gaps is in computing speed: There are 35 orders of magnitude between the technology’s current state and its limit. That’s equivalent to the difference between a nanosecond and 200 million times the age of the universe. It is also the least bridgeable gap of the four. To close it you would have to find a completely different way to build a computer, one that could compute with the entire energy contained in a lump of matter. Quantum computers could get us part of the way there if they could convert every degree of freedom in a lump of matter—every atom, and every way it can move or spin—into a computing element that we could reliably manipulate. In practice, current quantum computers go the other way, spending a lot of matter to create each computing element. Trillions of atoms go into each quantum bit, or qubit, the quantum counterpart of the bit in an ordinary computer. Because every qubit is fragile, dozens to thousands of them must be woven together to make a single one reliable enough for useful computation. In 1959, Richard Feynman offered a $1,000 prize to the first person to make a motor 1/64th of an inch on a side. William McLellan, a Caltech-trained engineer, soon fabricated one by hand under a microscope. This image shows an enlarged demonstration model (right). GETTY IMAGES Energy is where the floor is nearest. Today’s chips operate less than six orders of magnitude above the Landauer minimum. Conventional computing logic can close only part of that gap. A reliable switch has to be flipped by an amount of energy large enough that thermal fluctuations never flip it by accident, and that margin pins the transistor a hundred to a few thousand times above Landauer no matter how it is refined. But there are ideas for getting that energy lower by changing the physics of the computation. In 1973, IBM’s Charles Bennett showed that any computation can be arranged to throw nothing away. Such a reversible computation pays no erasure toll at all, because every step can be run backward to recover what went in. This approach is called adiabatic or reversible logic, and the first commercial attempts are now underway. For example, Vaire Computing, a startup founded to commercialize reversible logic, tested its first chip in 2025; the chip has resonant circuits that recover part of the switching energy instead of venting it as heat. Narrowing the memory density gap, meanwhile, would mean building devices that use all three dimensions at molecular scale. The most concrete example is DNA, which stores information at the scale of its own atoms, and which biology has used as a storage medium for 4 billion years. Feynman, being conservative, guessed that a single bit would require a cube of 125 atoms. DNA holds it in about 30. What keeps DNA storage out of the data center is not its density but the cost and speed of writing it, still many orders of magnitude from anything practical. The library in a dust speck that Feynman imagined is permitted by physics and held back only by fabrication. Communication sits about six orders of magnitude—just a factor of a million—from the Holevo limit, which is the threshold the industry will likely meet first. Interconnects are multiplying faster than the grid can power them, so the industry is moving to transmitters and receivers that use less energy per bit. Nvidia and Broadcom now ship optical interconnects built right against the silicon, so a signal leaves the chip package already on photons. Quantum computers, by comparison, are beginning to rely on interconnects that encode information on quantum signals, usually in the form of single photons. As classical interconnects spend fewer resources on each bit, they descend toward the regime where these quantum interconnects already operate. The Holevo limit is where the two will meet. It is fair to object that a gap of 35 orders of magnitude is a mirage—that a limit so remote says nothing about what any real machine will ever do, and that pointing to it is like navigating by the horizon. The objection has teeth. Reversible logic, quantum computing, and DNA storage have each been perpetually 10 years away for 40 years. And it will likely never be practical to build a computer that uses all the energy in a lump of matter. But these gaps are invitations. There is a ceiling, set by how much we can build: the number of devices we can fabricate; the power we can generate to run them; and the capital, land, and cooling water we can assemble into a single system. And there is a floor, set by how much a single joule, a single second, and a single gram of matter can be made to compute, store, or transmit. We can progress by building more or by approaching the floor, which means making each device do more with less. These gaps are invitations. We can progress by building more or by approaching the floor, which means making each device do more with less. For most of the last century, we proceeded down both paths together. We built more computers, and the computers themselves grew smaller and better. Now we mostly build more, and the ceiling is coming into view. A power grid can carry only so many gigawatts, and a region can spare only so much land and water. Yet every road map for what comes next is drawn from the same starting point: the machines we already have. Build more of them and you climb toward the ceiling; build better ones and you descend a little further, but only as far as the transistor’s own floor. There is a third direction. Start with a physics experiment operating at the floor and build up. It has been done before. The transistor was a physics experiment before it was an industry; the laser was a laboratory curiosity before it carried the world’s conversations under the ocean; giant magnetoresistance went from physics discovery to the read head of every disk drive within a decade. In each case, the physics experiment came first and showed what was possible, and engineers then turned it into a machine that can be scaled up. Building the experiments that operate at these fundamental limits, and then scaling them up without losing that performance, is the work that remains. The next machines will not be reached by descent; they will be built from the bottom up. There is still plenty of room at the bottom. articles.title: Open Source Protocol Deploys Cloudflare Edge to Run WhatsApp Model Context Agents
articles.content: Let your AI agent read your WhatsApp messages. This is a small server that runs in your own Cloudflare account. You link your phone to it once, the way you'd link WhatsApp Web, and from then on any MCP client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, anything that speaks MCP) can search and read your chats. It can read and search your messages, and remember names you give it for phone numbers. It can't send anything. Ask your agent things like: "What did Dana say about the flights?" "Find every message where someone mentioned the lease, across all my chats." "Summarize what I missed in the family group this week." Your phone stays the source of truth. The server is a linked device that your agent talks to. It doesn't stay connected to WhatsApp. When your agent asks for something, and once a day, it connects, collects whatever WhatsApp queued for it since last time, writes that to its own database, and hangs up. Your phone keeps working normally and keeps getting notifications. Your messages live in a SQLite database inside a Durable Object in your Cloudflare account. Nothing goes anywhere else. You need a Cloudflare account on the Workers Paid plan (see the note below), Node 20 or later, and your phone. git clone https://github.com/finereli/whatsapp-mcp cd whatsapp-mcp npm install # 1. A place for the sign-in tokens. Paste the id it prints into wrangler.jsonc. npx wrangler kv namespace create OAUTH_KV # 2. A password for the page that links your phone. 12+ characters. npx wrangler secret put OWNER_PASSWORD # 3. Deploy. npm run deploy Wrangler prints your URL, something like https://whatsapp-mcp.your-name.workers.dev . Open it. The front page has the two remaining steps: Link WhatsApp. Scan the QR code with WhatsApp (Settings, Linked Devices, Link a Device). If you're on the phone itself and can't scan a screen, use the phone number option instead. The first link imports your history. The page shows progress, and you can close it. Connect your agent. In Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http whatsapp https://your-url/mcp Then type /mcp and sign in with the password. Other clients: point them at the same /mcp URL. If you want your own domain, see the comments at the bottom of wrangler.jsonc . Importing a large history decodes a lot of data in one go, and the default CPU limit on Workers is too small for it. wrangler.jsonc raises it, and raising it needs the paid plan, which is a few dollars a month. I haven't tried the free plan. If you're on it, remove the limits block and expect the first import to be fragile. This isn't official. WhatsApp has no API for reading your own personal messages. This uses the same protocol WhatsApp Web uses, through an open source library (Baileys). That's against WhatsApp's terms. For a linked device that only reads, the practical risk is low, but it isn't zero. Use it on your own account, and don't use it to send messages. You get what WhatsApp sends. The first link imports whatever history WhatsApp decides to hand a new device. It may not be everything. It only does this once per link. To import again, relink (your stored messages are kept, and a re-import fills in anything missing). Some chats show up as phone numbers. WhatsApp doesn't give a linked device every contact name, and most of these are one-off messages from people you never saved. For the ones that matter, your agent can fix it: it lists the unnamed chats, looks the numbers up in your contacts with whatever contacts tool it already has (a Google Contacts or Gmail connector, for example), and saves the names. The server never connects to a contacts service itself. See "Naming chats" below. Media isn't downloaded. Photos, voice notes and documents appear as labels like [image] or [voice note 12s] , with the caption if there was one. Nothing is transcribed. It's for one person. One deployment is one WhatsApp account and one owner. That's deliberate: each deployment holds a full message history and a live login to the account, so everyone should run their own. Relinking. If your phone says the device was removed, or you want to start over, ask your agent to run relink , or open /setup and choose "Unlink and scan again". You scan a new QR code. Stored messages are kept. Tool What it does list_chats Chats, most recent first. Filter by name or number. get_messages Read one chat. Page back or forward by date. search_messages Full-text search across everything, or within one chat. unnamed_chats Chats known only by phone number, busiest first, with the last thing the other person said. set_contact_names Save names for phone numbers, in any format. Names stick to the number, so they also show up in groups. sync_now Pull new messages right now. link_status Is it linked, when did it last pull, how much is stored. relink Unlink and start over. A human has to scan the new QR code. Every read tool first tops up from WhatsApp if the stored copy is more than ten minutes old. WhatsApp only gives this server the names it knows. The rest show up as phone numbers. Rather than have the server log in to a contacts service (which means a cloud project, consent screens and, for Google, an app review), it hands the job to your agent, which usually already has a way to reach your contacts. Say "find names for my unnamed chats". The agent calls unnamed_chats , matches the numbers against your contacts, and saves what it finds with set_contact_names . It won't find everyone: most unnamed chats are a single message from a stranger. Agents get nudged toward this on their own. The server's instructions mention it, and so does every "no chat found" and "no matches" result, because that's the moment an agent is stuck on a name. link_status also says how many chats are unnamed. Everything below is for whoever is changing the code, including an AI agent working on a fork. The top of this file is for the person who owns the deployment. MCP client ──OAuth──> Worker (src/index.ts) ├─ /mcp ───────────> mcp.ts: tools, one fresh McpServer per request ├─ /, /setup, /authorize, /login/*, /pair/* (landing, sign-in, pairing UI) └─ cron 04:00 UTC ──> pull() │ RPC v WhatsAppStore (Durable Object, one instance named "owner") ├─ SQLite: auth keys, messages, chats, contacts, FTS5 index └─ Baileys socket, opened only during a session (pairing or pull) │ WebSocket v WhatsApp servers One Durable Object holds everything. Its SQLite is both the Baileys auth store and the message store. The Worker is stateless apart from a KV namespace the OAuth provider uses for tokens and a short-lived "pending sign-in" record. File Job src/index.ts Routes. OAuth provider wiring, sign-in, pairing endpoints, /debug , cron. src/auth.ts Who counts as the owner. Two modes: a password, or a login service. Also the owner's browser session. src/phone.ts Phone numbers in any format to WhatsApp jids. src/whatsapp-do.ts The Durable Object. Runs Baileys sessions, exposes RPC methods for the Worker. src/store.ts Schema, ingesting Baileys events into SQLite, and every query. src/auth-state.ts Baileys auth state backed by the DO's SQLite (replaces useMultiFileAuthState ). src/mcp.ts The MCP tools, and the hint that points agents at the naming tools. src/pages.ts , src/landing.ts , src/privacy.ts , src/tos.ts , src/ui.ts All HTML. ui.ts has the shared design tokens. src/ws-shim.ts , src/lru-shim.ts , src/polyfills.ts Make Baileys run on workerd. See below. scripts/vendor-bridge.mjs Extracts the wasm from Baileys' Rust bridge. Runs on npm install . local-export/ A separate one-off script that dumps your history to JSON files with no server. Not part of the deployment. All WhatsApp traffic happens inside runSession() in whatsapp-do.ts . There are two kinds: Pairing ( startPairing ). No credentials yet. Baileys emits QR strings, kept in memory and rendered to SVG by pairStatus() . After a scan WhatsApp closes the socket with code 515 (restart required), and the session reconnects with the new credentials. History arrives as messaging-history.set chunks with a progress percentage. The session ends when WhatsApp reports 100 percent and the stream has been quiet for a few seconds. Pull ( pull ). Reconnects with stored credentials. WhatsApp delivers whatever it queued while we were away, then signals receivedPendingNotifications . The session ends after a few quiet seconds. Callers share one session: a second pull() while one is running gets the same promise. A pairing session outlives the HTTP request that started it. startPairing sets a Durable Object alarm, and alarm() awaits the session promise. An in-flight alarm handler is what keeps the object alive. The pairing page only watches; closing it doesn't stop the import. Idle detection counts only data events ( messaging-history.set , messages.upsert ), not connection chatter. Counting everything keeps a session open forever, because presence and contact updates never stop. All in the Durable Object's SQLite ( store.ts , initSchema ). messages(chat, id, ts, from_me, sender, push_name, type, body) , primary key (chat, id) . Media is a label in body . Edits update body ; deletes set it to [deleted] . messages_fts , an FTS5 index over body , kept in sync by triggers. chats(jid, name, is_group) , contacts(jid, name, notify) and custom_names(jid, name) . Display names resolve by WhatsApp's chat name, then WhatsApp's contact name, then a saved name, then the person's own push name, then the number. custom_names is what set_contact_names writes. alias(lid, pn) . WhatsApp is moving to anonymous @lid identifiers. This maps them to phone-number JIDs, and addAlias folds existing rows into the phone-number form so one person is one chat. auth(k, v) , Baileys credentials and signal keys, JSON with Buffers encoded by Baileys' BufferJSON . meta(k, v) , currently just last_pull . Ingest is idempotent. Re-importing history upserts: it fills in a missing sender or push_name and never duplicates. That is what makes relinking safe. These all cost real time to find. Read them before touching the Baileys parts. Baileys needs three shims to run on workerd. ws : the package needs Node sockets. ws-shim.ts wraps the Workers WebSocket, opened with fetch() and an Upgrade header because that's the only way to set the Origin header WhatsApp checks. whatsapp-rust-bridge : it ships its wasm as base64 and compiles it at runtime, which workerd forbids. vendor-bridge.mjs writes the wasm to a file and patches the loader to import it as a CompiledWasm module. The vendor/ folder is generated, not committed. Timers: Node timers have .unref() and workerd's don't. polyfills.ts adds it. It must be the first import in both the Worker and the Durable Object module. lru-cache autopurge breaks the first import. Baileys creates caches with ttlAutopurge: true , which starts one setTimeout per entry. workerd allows 10,000 pending timers per object, and the first history sync blows through that with QuotaExceededError . lru-shim.ts turns autopurge off. Expired entries are still dropped lazily on access. QR pairing never sets creds.registered . That flag belongs to the mobile registration flow. "Is this linked" is creds.me?.id . History comes once per link. If a first import fails halfway, that history is gone until you relink. Don't ship a change to ingest code without testing it against a real first link. Group senders arrive in two places. Live messages have key.participant . History messages put it on msg.participant . Read both. Pin Baileys exactly. It's a prerelease and its API moves between release candidates. Deploys don't evict a busy Durable Object. An object with an active session keeps running old code until the session ends. Renaming the class with a migration didn't evict it either. If you've shipped a fix and the object still misbehaves, stop sending it requests and wait three to five minutes. Every probe, including /debug , resets its idle timer, so polling a stale object keeps it stale. Baileys also leaks interval timers when a socket closes; finish() in whatsapp-do.ts clears them so the object can go idle at all. Logging out takes two steps. logout() first connects and calls Baileys' logout() , so the device disappears from the phone's list, then clears local credentials. If the first step fails it says so in the debug events, and the user has to remove the device by hand. WhatsApp stores a placeholder where a name should be. Chats it has no contact for are named after the number, sometimes masked ( +972∙∙∙∙∙∙∙20 ), in the chat name and the contact name. numberLike in store.ts treats those as no name, and ingest refuses to store them. Before that fix a placeholder outranked a real saved name. Don't call markOnlineOnConnect . It's set to false on purpose. Marking the linked device online makes the phone stop showing notifications. Name Kind Purpose OWNER_PASSWORD secret Password mode (default). 12+ characters or sign-in refuses. OWNER_EMAIL var Login-service mode: the one email allowed in. OPERATOR_NAME var, optional Shown on the privacy page as who runs this server. DEFAULT_COUNTRY_CODE var, optional Country code (digits, no plus), used when your agent saves a number written without one, e.g. 972 . LOGIN_ORIGIN var Set this to switch to login-service mode. ALLOWED_ORIGINS var Login-service mode: comma-separated origins whose tokens are accepted. Production should list only production. PIN secret, optional 32+ random characters. Enables the /debug routes via an x-pin header. Leave it unset to leave them off. OAUTH_KV binding Token store for the OAuth provider and pending sign-ins. WA binding The Durable Object. Keep a deployment's own values (domain, KV id, email) in wrangler.local.jsonc , which is gitignored, and deploy with npm run deploy:local . wrangler.jsonc is the template other people start from. Add a tool. Register it in mcp.ts and put the SQL in store.ts . Read tools should call fresh() first. Keep tools read-only unless you mean otherwise. If a failure leaves an agent stuck, say in the tool result what to try next, the way NAME_HINT does for missing names. Change who can sign in. auth.ts picks a mode ( authMode ) and the routes in index.ts follow it. To add another identity provider, add a mode there and a callback route. The rest of the code only sees an opaque bearer token. Make it multi-user. Today the Durable Object is addressed by the fixed name owner ( wa() in index.ts , handleMcp in mcp.ts ), and userId is the constant 'owner' in the OAuth props. To go multi-user, derive both from the signed-in identity and key the object on it. Think about whether you want to hold other people's message history first. Other ways to fill in names. Anything that can produce { jid, name } rows can call store.setCustomNames . A CSV upload, a CardDAV pull or a scheduled job would all work. The agent route exists so the server needs no credentials for any of them. Sending messages. Not built, on purpose. Think hard before adding it. With PIN set, these return JSON and need the header x-pin: <PIN> : /debug : session phase, linked or not, counts, and the last events from the session (connection changes, history chunk sizes, errors). /debug/pull : run a pull now. /debug/chats?q= , /debug/messages?chat= , /debug/search?q= , /debug/types : read the store without going through MCP. /debug/unnamed : the chats unnamed_chats would return. /debug/sql?q= : one read-only SELECT against the store, for finding out why a name or a count looks wrong. /debug/logout : the same as relink . Local development: npm run dev with a .dev.vars containing OWNER_PASSWORD=... (12+ characters). It runs a local Durable Object with its own empty storage, so you can exercise the sign-in flow and see a real QR code, but linking a phone from local dev makes a second linked device. To test the pairing UI states without a phone, serve the page with a mocked /pair/status . Everything the page needs is that one JSON shape: paired , running , progress , qrSvg , messages , chats . npm run typecheck , then npm test . The test runs the real store code against Node's built-in SQLite (Node 22.13 or later), including the migration from older versions. That SQLite has no FTS5, so search itself isn't covered. Deploy, then GET /debug with the PIN. It should come back with phase: "idle" and paired: true . GET /debug/pull . A quiet account should return reason: "idle" in about ten seconds. Call list_chats , then get_messages on a Hebrew or emoji-heavy chat, then search_messages . Then unnamed_chats , and set_contact_names on one number, and confirm the chat shows the name. If you touched ingest, relink and confirm the stored message count doesn't grow (re-import is idempotent) and that group messages show real sender names. Chats with no name in WhatsApp and none saved show as phone numbers. Nothing refreshes names by itself: they only get saved when an agent (or you) does it. If the daily pull finds the session logged out, nothing tells you. link_status shows it the next time your agent asks. Edits and deletes are applied when they arrive as protocol messages. That path hasn't been tested against real ones. It's only been exercised against one real account. MIT

articles.title: Paris Urban Riots Stymie Olympic Facial Recognition Enforcement Deployments
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Protesters loot a supermarket amid clashes during a day of demonstrations against the cost of living and rising fuel prices in Paris, France, on Oct 17. PHOTO: REUTERS Published Oct 19, 2026, 12:52 AM Updated Oct 19, 2026, 01:36 AM Set as preferred source Listen PARIS - French police battled protesters and looters for a second day on Oct 18 as the country reeled from the violent chaos left by a day of cost-of-living demonstrations in which 2,000 people were arrested nationwide. Paris city workers had not finished clearing up the torched cars, smashed shopfronts and burnt debris from the unrest on Oct 17 when the new troubles started and political recriminations erupted. AFP journalists said several hundred people gathered in the Republique square in the capital following social media calls for a gathering that the authorities said had not been approved. Television footage showed the looting of a clothing store and bikes were also set alight nearby. The Paris police prefecture said security forces moved in when “faced with the initial signs of tension”. A fire burns as Police officers in riot gear stand guard during civil unrest in Paris, France on Oct 18. PHOTO: REUTERS AFP journalists saw police firing tear gas and stun grenades at hundreds of people gathered in the square. Bottles and rocks were hurled at police who made several arrests. Some 550 people out of 855 arrested in Paris remained in detention from Oct 17’s troubles and police stations were struggling to cope, according to the Legal Team Paris group of lawyers. Six months from a presidential election, the government faced opposition attacks over preparations for the nationwide day of action that followed weeks of mounting student protests over conditions in schools . President Emmanuel Macron, who on Oct 17 vowed that anyone who engaged in vandalism or looting would be prosecuted, was to address the nation on the evening of Oct 18. Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate for the National Rally party, said the troubles showed that Macron’s administration was “running on fumes, exhausted and disoriented”. “We are experiencing a profound crisis of trust and authority, which poses a threat to democracy,” said Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of the election. Le Pen has blamed ultra-left groups, while Jean-Luc Melenchon head of the far-left France Unbowed party accused authorities of inflaming tensions. A municipal worker, seen through a burnt-out car, cleans a street on Oct 18, a day after the protests. PHOTO: REUTERS With images of French town halls burning and shops being looted grabbing headlines around the world, US President Donald Trump waded into the debate , blaming immigration for the unrest. “France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,” Trump said in a social media post. Looting rampages were reported on Oct 17 in Paris and other cities, including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Strasbourg, on the margins of protests over the cost of living. Around 1,500 businesses were damaged with losses estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars, according to the Retail and Trade Federation. One person died during the main march in Paris, but officials said the case was health-related. “It’s like we had a war,” a 78-year-old Paris resident Mehmet Ozeden told AFP amid burnt street barricades from the protests. Another resident, Anita Gras, said she saw young men loot a sports shoe retailer. “It’s appalling, terrifying – groups of young people came here yesterday, looting, smashing everything, with total impunity,” said 57-year-old Cecile Rogue surveying a pile of charred bicycles. The city of Limoges lost its 19th-century town hall to a fire that local prefect, Maurice Barate, told news channel LCI had been deliberately set by “a wild horde”. About 7,000 people staged a march in the central city on Oct 18 to show their anger at the devastation. In Lyon, a store owner, Jean-Christian, said those behind the violence were “animals”. “We saw them looting, men high on adrenaline.” A tourist office in the city centre was set ablaze during the protests amid multiple clashes and looting. On Oct 18, a clothing store was also looted in Lyon. In Paris, startled tourists were seen on Oct 17 running with suitcases along streets filled with tear gas and protesters. Tourists run with their luggages near place de La Madeleine and a fire during the protests in Paris on Oct 17. PHOTO: AFP A Danish tourist, Soren Petersen, said it was “sad” to see damage to Paris buildings. “It is not a protest, it’s far beyond a normal protest,” he told AFP. Around 500 police, firefighters and paramedics were hurt in the protests, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. The violence took place on the sidelines of nationwide protests that the interior ministry said drew 550,000 people. The CGT union said 800,000 people participated. A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Etienne. In Mulhouse a 17-year-old girl lost an eye, according to prosecutors. France’s Yellow Vest movement, which staged street protests eight years ago against Macron’s government over planned fuel-tax hikes, had called Saturday’s “yellow and youth” demonstrations. AFP Police France Jordan

articles.title: South African Freight Rail Collapse Strangles Automotive Export Corridors
articles.content: If everyone involved was being honest, Pretoria’s location made it a bad place to set up a carmaking hub. But it can become the gateway to Africa if all the stakeholders, especially the state, work at it. By Lindsey Schutters 18 Oct 2026 Ford Motor Company’s logo as seen on 13 January 2022 at its plant in Silverton, Pretoria. (File photo: Fani Mahuntsi / Gallo Images) Dive Deeper Speed Read Summary Listen Dive Deeper There was a blue, oval-shaped void on the show floor at SA Auto Week 2026 in Durban this week. Ford Motor Company Africa’s president, Neale Hill, was on the speakers’ list, but it had no representation as a brand with a stand. Into this vacuum stepped Chery, latest tenant of the Nissan factory in Rosslyn, Pretoria, and its neighbour in the not-so-special automotive economic zone, BMW. The Eastern Cape can say what it wants, but Gauteng hosts 200 automotive component firms alongside major assembly plants, and generates 34.4% of South Africa’s total GDP. And Pretoria serves as the country’s central hub for automotive research, development and technical skills, making a powerful case for it serving as the strategic inland platform for vehicle assembly and export into broader African markets. Tony Liu, chief executive of Chery SA, says that as a new investor coming to the country, the company is in it for the long run. “We are here in South Africa for the people and are also becoming a South African citizen. So, we are part of the economy, part of this country’s economic development.” But there are barriers that all businesses and even citizens fully understand, and Liu knows he will have to grapple with them. “Infrastructure-cost competitiveness, including water and electricity – those are basic things. Logistics cost – that is also going to be adding a lot of weight onto our competitiveness across Africa and even globally,” he tells Daily Maverick. BMW’s Rosslyn plant exports most of its production volume. Operating far inland from coastal export ports creates structural logistics vulnerabilities that require reliable rail infrastructure and stable municipal grid connections. “It’s the wrong place, to be honest, because we export 96% of our volume… So that’s always been an issue, and our biggest challenges have been logistics,” admits Peter van Binsbergen, chairperson and chief executive of BMW Group SA. The Transnet curse One of the benefits of moving into Rosslyn is that a railway line runs by it, but this has not always been the benefit it should have been. “We’ve had a lot of logistics challenges in the time when Transnet was shaky,” says Van Binsbergen. “Post-Covid, when railway lines and power cables were being stolen, we had a lot of problems getting our cars and our parts in and out of Rosslyn. So we even brought in containers via Mozambique and things like that. “We have a rail line that comes right to our siding at the vehicle distribution centre, but that rail line has just been notoriously unstable.” Chery SA chief executive Tony Liu. (Photo: Supplied / Chery South Africa) So, Daily Maverick was not surprised to spot both Van Binsbergen and Liu in conversation with Transnet group CEO Michelle Phillips on day two of the conference. “We managed to clear up ... as the motor industry meeting with Transnet that we want to actually put more on rail instead of on trucks,” the BMW chief disclosed. “Trucks are not our wish… But you need to balance your line so that it’s full going down to the port and full coming back. Having Chery in Rosslyn might, or will, give us a bit more muscle to balance that line a bit better.” Special zone, special treatment One Pretoria carmaker that also has a railway line running right by it, Ford, was actually promised improved logistics when it sank R15-billion into Silverton. “There has been progress in the broader rail reform process, including the rail access framework and onboarding of private operators, as well as some progress at ports,” Ford wrote in reply to questions. “However, rail is one part of an interconnected logistics value chain, and the entire ecosystem needs to operate in unison. “For Ford, the key issue is how this translates into reliable, commercially viable services that support automotive manufacturing and exports. “This requires a rail system that runs on time, has suitable rolling stock, and provides dependable connections between manufacturing hubs and ports so that incoming goods and export vehicles reach their destinations on schedule, and support our wider business operations. Neale Hill, president of Ford Motor Company in Africa, at a function on 10 April 2024 when the Nelson Mandela Foundation recognised the company as a Legacy Champion, the highest tier of donors to the foundation. (Photo: Supplied) “Access agreements and reform milestones are important, but the real measure will be dependable operational services across the logistics chain.” Ford’s castle is in the heart of the Tshwane Automotive Special Economic Zone (Tasez), an empire that spans 162.6ha in Silverton and holds pride of place as Africa’s first automotive city. It is backed by direct funding and a multi- tiered government partnership between the De­­partment of Trade, Industry and Com­petition, the Gauteng provincial gov­­ernment and the City of Tshwane. As part of the privilege of re­­ceiving Cyril Rama­phosa’s blessing during his 2019 presidential campaign, the Tasez has been integrated into a VIP energy grid to protect tenants against municipal power interruptions, alongside dedicated rail sidings connecting Rosslyn and Silverton factories straight to export ports. Break in the chain Transnet’s CEO has actively engaged with automotive leaders during industry forums to build collaboration channels between the state-owned logistics provider and primary vehicle manufacturers. “We will talk to the automotive industry about how best we can support them going forward, both on port and rail, and engage with them on collaboration initiatives and how they can support us to make sure that we do what is required for the industry,” Phillips told Daily Maverick after her conversation with Liu. Transnet group CEO Michelle Phillips at the Africa Rail Expo that was held at the Sandton Convention Centre on 7 July 2026 in Johannesburg. (File photo: Fani Mahuntsi / Gallo Images) “We are in this business because we know that it’s difficult, actually, and that there are problems to be solved. I think in the logistics space, if you don’t have a problem, then you have a problem... Look, we are trying hard together with the teams to support the industry as much as we can.” To be fair to Transnet, it is on the right track to reform in two important ways. First, manufacturers acknowledge a marked improvement in Transnet’s willingness to communicate openly, resolving misunderstandings regarding rail usage versus road freighting. And second, Phillips’s engagement with Rosslyn manufacturers on bi-directional corridor efficiency addresses line balancing – using inbound trains for imported components or vehicles and outbound trains for export vehicles – and has seemingly set clear objectives. However, there is still an execution gap. Although leadership dialogue is welcomed, manufacturer evaluations – particularly from Ford – still show that reform milestones, access frameworks and private sector onboarding must rapidly translate into on-time rail schedules, sufficient rolling stock and seamless port handling to protect manufacturing competitiveness. Van Binsbergen reveals a possible policy direction that could salvage the ailing industry. “If we really want to get economies of scale, we’ve got to actually agree that [we need to] specialise in South Africa … in wiring harnesses, car glass, tyres,” he suggests. “And then we have to be able to talk to each other without breaking competition law to say, ‘Okay guys, these are the topics we’re going to focus on. We’re going to give enough ­volume to the producer so they can get their economies of scale in place and we can develop like pools of competence.’ ” There must be something in the water on the west side of Tshwane because Liu was singing a similar tune of collaboration and united industrial action. Now, if only that message can spread. DM This story first appeared in our weekly DM168 newspaper, available countrywide for R39.
